entries.title: Mike Rogers’ Pitch to Jewish Democrats May Be Falling Flat
entries.summary: The Republican has been trying to poach Jewish voters who are hesitant to support Democrat Abdul El-Sayed, but local leaders say they don’t see the pitch sticking.
entries.content:
Mike Rogers lost his Senate race in 2024 by fewer than 20,000 votes. Now, the Republican is ramping up efforts to pick off portions of historically Democratic coalitions in Michigan — including Jewish voters who draw a hard line on support for Israel.

The dynamics reflect a pressure point for progressive Democrats, who have had to tread carefully while speaking out against Israel as the party contends with growing divisions in a competitive midterm cycle. The Democratic nominee, Abdul El-Sayed, is one of the candidates most vocally critical of Israel running a statewide race this year, and battleground Michigan — which has some of the country’s largest Arab and Muslim populations — is a prime test for whether historically liberal communities will break from Democrats over the foreign policy debate.

This week, Rogers has ramped up his efforts to hone in on that corner of the electorate, including dropping a new ad on Tuesday centering a voter wearing a Star of David necklace who described herself as a “pissed off Democrat.” Furthermore, an open letter from Jewish Democrats started circulating Wednesday, in which signatories ask Jewish Democrats and independents to back Rogers over El-Sayed, who the Republican has called “beyond antisemitic” in the past.

But some experts, including Jewish political leaders in Michigan, say Rogers has a low chance of meaningfully peeling off support from the long-standing Democratic bloc.

“That letter does not reflect our caucus at all,” Decky Alexander, chair of the Michigan Democratic Jewish Caucus, told NOTUS. “We are not in the business of putting forth any kind of movement or initiative that would undermine the current slate of Democratic candidates.”

“I don't know if it's dangerous, but I find it shortsighted,” Alexander added. “I don't want people to think that it's reflecting this broad scope of the Jewish community because I don't believe it does.”

El-Sayed and other statewide candidates are set to speak at a late August event hosted by the caucus, which is an official branch of the state Democratic Party and backed Rep. Haley Stevens in the primary. Alexander says the group is waiting to throw its support behind El-Sayed, and would not do any further endorsements until after the Aug. 30 gathering.

If elected, El-Sayed says he would support an immediate arms embargo and oppose distributing “direct blank-check funding” to foreign militaries, including Israel. The candidate, who is the most prominent Muslim running statewide this year, has also gone out of his way to specifically condemn antisemitism.

“I want you to know that my commitment to your safety — my commitment to Jewish safety — is the same commitment that I have to the safety of my own daughters,” he told prospective voters the day after winning his primary.

This week’s open letter, first reported by Jewish Insider, describes Rogers as “a friend to the Jewish community” and asks voters to separate the Republican nominee from President Donald Trump.

“All of us have felt threatened and alienated by the politics and allies embraced by Abdul El-Sayed,” the letter, led by Detroit businessman Eric Bronstein, reads. “We cannot allow him to become the Democratic standard-bearer or Michigan’s senator.”

Bronstein did not respond to a request for comment. The group has not publicly released the full letter, and told Jewish Insider it plans to publish the letter online once it has gained “a significant initial group of signers.”

Rogers’ campaign has tried to capitalize on the divide in the meantime by courting Jewish voters, who nationally tend to support Democrats in large margins. He has featured Jewish faith leaders and members of the community on campaign stops.

"We’re grateful for the support from Jewish Democrats who’ve been ringing our phones off the hook asking what they can do and how they can get involved,” the Rogers campaign’s communications director, Alyssa Brouillet, told NOTUS.

Republicans are similarly trying to court the Jewish vote in other states like Georgia, where Rep. Mike Collins has tried to capitalize on Sen. Jon Ossoff’s criticism of the Israeli government — despite Ossoff’s moderate political views and his status as the state’s first Jewish senator. But El-Sayed’s campaign highlights how, particularly over the last three years, progressive Democrats have had to maneuver condemning Israel’s actions in Gaza while facing backlash from critics who say their comments are antisemitic.

Other left-leaning politicians like New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, who is also Muslim, have tried to tailor their messages to somewhat weather the storm of criticism — though El-Sayed is still addressing the fallout from his past comments on Israel-U.S. policy.

When asked by CNN in July if Israel has the right to exist, El-Sayed pushed back on the question, calling it a “gotcha game.”

“I think the question we all ought to ask is does everybody have equal rights to peace, dignity and self-determination? That’s Jewish Israelis and Palestinians,” he said later in the interview.

Midwest political strategist Adrian Hemond said one of El-Sayed’s top priorities ahead of the general election should be “giving a nonslippery answer” when asked sweeping questions about Israel’s right to exist.

“He's never given a direct answer to that question, and I think that concerns about his views will persist until he does,” Hemond told NOTUS, adding that he doesn’t think El-Sayed appears to have made a meaningful effort to engage with Jewish communities in the state.

El-Sayed campaign spokesperson Roxie Richner told NOTUS that the candidate remains in “regular dialogue” with local Jewish leaders in hopes of building the “broadest possible coalition.”

Alexander says she has been in contact with El-Sayed through her work with the caucus, which has been “inundated” with voters’ requests for conversations with the nominee. But she still thinks the Democrat needs to adjust his rhetoric and increase outreach with Jewish voters if he hopes to win in November — especially since he is “a better messenger for his own ideas than I am.”

“There is a lot of profound — and still is — anti-Israel and anti-Jewish rhetoric coming out of that campaign, and it has to be addressed more directly,” Alexander said. “It has to be addressed, otherwise people will continue to write more letters like that.”

In contrast to El-Sayed, Rogers has billed himself as a pro-Israel candidate, saying Israel has “every right to defend their nation” from threats. While the American Israel Public Affairs Committee spent a record-breaking amount to prop up Stevens during the Democratic primary, the group could mount another large spending campaign to support Rogers before November, The New York Times reported earlier this month.

There is limited polling on the views of Michigan’s Jewish voters, who comprise roughly 1.4% of the state’s electorate. A national Associated Press survey found that few Jewish adults see either party as highly supportive of their communities, and respondents were divided on whether criticism of Israel counts as antisemitic. Another poll of 500 Michigan Democrats, released three weeks before the primary, found that voters did not place a high level of importance on candidates' positions on Israel and Gaza when making their choice. Almost half had an unfavorable view of AIPAC.

Alexander and Theresa Reid, chair of the Washtenaw County Democratic Party — the county with one of the largest Jewish populations in the state — stressed that the issue is not monolithic and there is a significant diversity in thought among Jewish voters.

“I can tell you definitively that there is not one stance on this issue; the strategy conversation is very active,” Reid wrote in an email to NOTUS.

The Washtenaw County GOP’s chair, Jason Rogers, described the letter as “correct and necessary” and says he has spoken to a few Jewish Democrats that are planning to support Rogers.

“The Democratic Party has left the Jewish community behind. As Republicans we would welcome them into the real big-tent party,” Rogers wrote in an email. “Above all, allegiance to our Constitutional Republic comes first.”

In a swing state like Michigan, the power of a few thousand votes cannot be overlooked. Sen. Elissa Slotkin, a Jewish Democrat who positions herself as a moderate critic of Israel, bested Rogers in the 2024 senate race by less than a half a percentage point.

With 75 days until the general election, Alexander says the push to break Jewish voters away from El-Sayed doesn’t currently have real traction. While the Democratic candidate has some work to do, she said liberal voters know the stakes are high if they hope to break up Republicans’ control of the Senate.

“He's got to do some convincing — but also, you know, the state of the world might just do that convincing as well,” Alexander said.
entries.author: Jenna Monnin

entries.title: As IndyCar Roars Through D.C., Preservationists Raise Alarm
entries.summary: There is little public information about how vibrations created by the race could affect nearby landmarks and artworks.
entries.content:
More than 100,000 racing fans are expected to descend on the nation’s capital this weekend to watch as the streets around the National Mall become an IndyCar course. But not everyone is cheering.

Preservationists from across the country are worried about the side effects of the Freedom 250 Grand Prix, particularly the vibrations from race cars thundering at speeds in excess of 185 miles per hour past landmarks including the National Gallery of Art, the Smithsonian’s National Air and Space Museum and the Wilbur J. Cohen Federal Building. They say these vibrations could damage the precious treasures housed inside.

“I’ve been to an IndyCar race,” said Mary Okin, the assistant director of the Living New Deal, a nonprofit research project and public archive of New Deal history. “Your whole body shakes. You can blow out an eardrum.”

The National Gallery of Art, home to a massive Alexander Calder mobile suspended from the ceiling of its East Building, commissioned a vibration study to assess possible impacts. Though the museum would not give specifics, it has taken steps “to ensure the safety of our staff, visitors, collection and facilities during the race.”

Museum spokesperson Chris Abanavas emphasized that the measures were being taken out of a “great abundance of caution.”

Officials at several Smithsonian museums along the race course referred all inquiries to the central Smithsonian office, which responded with information about museums’ operating hours and entry procedures during the race and details of Grand Prix-related food specials that will be offered — including “high-octane lattes” — but not to questions about the impact of the race on their collections.

Officials at the National Archives also did not respond to requests for comment.

Drivers in the first-ever race to take over the streets of the nation’s capital will run 147 laps — roughly 250 miles — around the 1.7-mile, seven-turn course. There will be practice sessions and qualifying events on Saturday before the race on Sunday, which will begin on Pennsylvania Avenue near the U.S. Capitol.

President Trump has been among the event’s biggest boosters.

“It’ll be an awesome display of American patriotism and raw horsepower, ingenuity,” he said during the Freedom Grand Prix Showcase last month. “They’re going to go all around the National Mall at speeds … if we did that during the regular day, I think people would be put in jail, perhaps, for the rest of their lives.”

Okin raised her concerns in a letter sent to the National Park Service last month. In the letter, first reported by the New Republic, Okin wrote that vibrations from the high-speed race could cause an “adverse effect” on historic properties under federal preservation rules.

“This is unprecedented,” said Michelle Arcari Rose, a former associate general counsel at the National Trust for Historic Preservation. “Why would we risk it? Why would you do it repeatedly over the course of two days, when we know there’s super fragile art that can’t be moved?”

Okin has urged officials to install low-cost vibration monitors on murals at the Cohen Building to measure whether the works are harmed by speeding cars but has received no response.

“You don’t have to be an expert to know fragile murals and race cars don’t mix,” Okin said.

In a statement, the General Services Administration, which oversees and manages real estate for the federal government, said it conducted a review of the proposed route and identified “no areas of concern.”

Some precautionary measures, however, have been taken. More than 200 manhole covers have been welded down to prevent them from flying loose during the race.

The National Park Service referred all inquiries to the Freedom 250 Grand Prix organizers, who did not respond to a request for comment. However, in a March 20 letter to David Maloney, D.C.’s state historic preservation officer, the agency’s National Mall and Memorial Parks unit concluded the race would have no adverse effect on historic properties. The D.C. planning office concurred in a letter dated April 21. But Arcari Rose and Okin say a more in-depth examination of the potential impact should have taken place.

As the popularity of motor sports has increased, more cities have sought to host such events. But some historic preservationists argue that certain venues are better suited to hosting them than others.

“I don’t think that anyone feels like having races on the streets of Las Vegas is inappropriate,” said Susan Kern, the director of the historic preservation program at the University of Maryland School of Architecture, Planning and Preservation. “This feels inappropriate.”

“These older structures were not designed with this in mind,” she added. “[It’s] shortsighted.”

Trump first laid the groundwork for this weekend’s events in January, when he signed an executive order, “Celebrating American Greatness with American Motor Racing,” establishing the race as one of several events celebrating the 250th anniversary of the signing of the Declaration of Independence. Now, the race has arrived and the District is bracing for a one-of-a-kind event.

“Reasonable people would not risk this,” said Arcari Rose. “I call this a Jurassic Park problem. Just because you can bring back the dinosaurs doesn’t mean that it’s a good idea. Just because you can do something doesn’t mean you should do it.”
entries.author: Lori Aratani

entries.title: Bracing for the Racing
entries.content:
Good morning. This is the NOTUS Metro newsletter for Aug. 21, 2026. You can get it in your inbox every day by signing up here — it’s free!

THE LATEST

D.C.’s first-ever IndyCar race has literally pulled into the station.

Ahead of the Freedom 250 Grand Prix, which takes place Sunday with practice sessions and qualifiers Saturday, a racecar was paraded along Metro’s Yellow Line on Thursday.

Perhaps the car took the Metro to avoid traffic. While racecars this weekend will fly by at speeds in excess of 185 mph, some D.C. drivers complained this week about hourslong commutes due to race-related road closures. Officials — and your friends at NOTUS — are highly encouraging folks to use Metro instead.

The honking horns of traffic are nothing compared with the noise that this weekend’s event is expected to create. A typical IndyCar race produces around 110-130 decibels of noise, per Washingtonian magazine. That’s just under the threshold of pain. Other things that produce a similar level: nightclubs, ambulance sirens, rock concerts, vuvuzelas, jackhammers and jet engines heard from 100 meters.

The racecars also create thundering vibrations, and these worry some preservationists, Lori Aratani reports for NOTUS. Cars will speed past several landmarks housing plenty of artwork, including the National Gallery of Art, the Smithsonian’s National Air and Space Museum and the Wilbur J. Cohen Federal Building.

“Reasonable people would not risk this,” one preservationist said. “I call this a Jurassic Park problem. … Just because you can do something doesn’t mean you should do it.”





FROM THE DISTRICT

Chuck Brown’s relatives are wound up. The family of D.C.’s Godfather of Go-Go took to Instagram on Thursday to express their frustration over how the city has managed the annual Chuck Brown Day festivities, which are scheduled for this weekend.

"After three years of being marginalized in both the planning process and the overall direction of the event, we no longer believe the event reflects the level of collaboration, respect, and stewardship that Chuck Brown's legacy deserves," a statement from the family reads. Until new leadership is found for the popular event, the family says they will no longer take part.

Vaccination rates among D.C. kindergartners decreased last school year, according to new CDC data reported by Axios D.C. The change is part of a national trend, with a backdrop of continued efforts by President Donald Trump’s administration to roll back vaccine requirements.

Test scores are up again in D.C. schools, per results from the city’s annual assessments that were released this week. Proficiency in English stands at 39.6%, up 2 percentage points from last year, while math proficiency is up to 28.5%, a gain of 2.1 percentage points. City officials say this is the fourth consecutive year of proficiency gains. Still, improvements were more pronounced in lower grades than in higher ones, and significant gaps exist between different demographic groups.





FROM MARYLAND

Not so fast: Montgomery County is testing a program that would catch drivers who speed through intersections on green lights, WTOP reports. The county is updating two of its 76 red-light cameras, both in Silver Spring, to try it out later this year.





METRO MOMENTS


2002 DC Race (2272x1704, AR: 1.33)
Earlier this week, we wrote about the 2002 American Le Mans series race that took place in the parking lots at RFK Stadium — that was the last time the District hosted a racing event at the scale we’ll see this weekend. 

We heard from reader Scot Hasselman, who not only attended that 2002 race but took plenty of pictures in the crowd. Here’s one of our favorites, featuring a background appearance from the Metro. Thank you to Scot for sending those over! 




SPORTS

Mystics rookie Georgia Amoore has struggled of late, posting three zero-point performances in her last five outings. That’s not good enough for a starting point guard, especially one on a young, playoff-contending team. But, as NOTUS’ Dave Sheinin reports, Washington has rallied around its court general, publicly highlighting contributions that can’t be seen on a stats sheet and giving her the time and space to improve.

What to Watch Today

MLB: Nationals at Marlins, 7:10 (MLB.TV)

WNBA: Mystics vs. Lynx, 7:30 (Ion)





Thank you for reading! If you liked this newsletter, please forward it to a friend. If someone shared it with you, please sign up — it’s free! Got a tip or comments to share? Email us at metro@notus.com.

The newsletter was produced by Jaden Amos, Michael Errigo and Nikie Johnson.

entries.title: The Transformed OIG
entries.content:
Today’s notice: Inspectors general have changed. One politician really loved their test ride for the Freedom 250. Michael Cohen and Donald Trump reunited. Who’s watching Sean Duffy’s reality show? And: The voters Democrats really need this fall might be the ones who vote third party.  





THE LATEST

Independent no more. How different are inspectors general offices under Trump 2.0? NOTUS’ Natalie Alms and Eric Katz report that the once-independent system Congress established after Watergate has been radically transformed — including with a potentially pricey bathroom renovation.

The new crop of IGs. Veterans Affairs IG Cheryl Mason was previously VA Secretary Doug Collins’ top adviser. As IG, she held up a planned office move over her demand for a personal lavatory, staffers said. She also commissioned a flag for herself, telling staff she was serving in the equivalent role of a four-star general and therefore required one. One OIG employee said the flag cost more than $1,000.

In meetings, Mason boasts of her personal relationship to Collins, and she confirmed she’s canceled so-called public “preliminary alerts” of IG findings after complaints about them from Collins’ staff. “It’s not about gotcha with the department,” Mason said of her role.

This is a common approach now. At HUD, acting IG Brian Harrison told his team in a meeting, “The independence of the inspector general is intended to lessen friction, not increase friction,” according to a recording obtained by NOTUS.

At the Labor Department, IG Anthony D’Esposito, a former Republican congressman, fired the career staffer who headed investigations in his office almost immediately after taking the job, NOTUS learned. That person had been spearheading a probe into an alleged inappropriate relationship between then-Labor Secretary Lori Chavez-DeRemer and a staffer.

Veterans of the gig are dismayed. Former Labor IG Larry Turner was fired and replaced by D’Esposito after a career that spanned four different IG offices. He’s never seen an inspector general “acting as an extension of a Cabinet member” like he perceives D’Esposito to be. “What message does it say to your staff?” he said.

Open tabs: Democrat Aisha Wahab Wins Special Election to Replace Eric Swalwell (NOTUS); U.S. Workers Are Paying More for Healthcare, and Next Year Will Be Worse (WSJ); GOP issues stark warning to AI companies (Axios); Invited media and military members held at gunpoint at Space Force base (AP)





From the District


Race to the 250 finish line. When the IndyCar engines come to life for the Freedom 250 Grand Prix this weekend, it will be the president’s last chance to unify the country in patriotic fervor after several other America 250 events fell flat.

Donald Trump created the big race — 147 laps around a 1.7-mile track, making it just about 250 total miles around the National Mall — through an executive order in January. Many in Washington are dreading the event. Lori Aratani writes for NOTUS today about preservationists freaking out at the prospect of grand prix vibrations in the vicinity of all the old and fragile things the nation keeps on the Mall.

Event Chair Bud Denker, the Penske Corporation president, told NOTUS’ Manuela Silva that he had been able to assuage many people’s concerns. In 93 days, he had 81 meetings on Capitol Hill, he told her. And in a rare feat in Congress, he said he “never left an office where someone didn’t think [the grand prix] was a good idea.”

One way he lobbied for the race was behind the wheel of a white Corvette. He’s taken Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and a few other VIPs around the track, and gotten good reviews.

“One hundred miles an hour down Pennsylvania Avenue,” Denker recalled of his outing with outgoing D.C. Mayor Muriel Bowser. “She was so scared. … I took off like a crazy man, and she’s just in the Corvette and she wouldn’t say anything, and then her dress started flying in the air because we were in a convertible.”

He showed NOTUS a text from the mayor where she thanked him for the “time of her life.” Asked for comment, Bowser’s office said she’ll be riding around the track again this morning.

From “The Michael Cohen Show”


The song was played. “Reunited (And It Feels So Good)” by Peaches & Herb played under part of former Trump fixer-turned-turncoat-turned-supporter Michael Cohen’s softball interview with the president, which appeared to solidify a reconciliation between the pair. “I respect the fact that you recanted everything you said,” Trump told Cohen.

From the open road


Low turnout for ‘The Great American Road Trip.’ NOTUS’ Emily Kennard was one of only around 8,500 total YouTube viewers of Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy’s reality series as of 5 p.m. yesterday, despite the series’ corporate sponsors spending millions of dollars on the show’s production.

The show features appearances from Trump and Interior Secretary Doug Burgum. It largely focuses on Duffy’s children — there are nine — and the family is often shown driving in two separate SUVs. A message of confidence in a summer of $4/gallon gas?





NOTUS PERSPECTIVES

Dana Milbank looks at how data centers are destroying Virginia’s countryside — even in places that have no data centers.





NOTUS METRO

Sign up for our local newsletter, written by Martin Austermuhle and Zara Norman.

Sports desk: The Mystics Value Georgia Amoore’s Intangibles. They’d Also Gladly Take More Points. By Dave Sheinin





NEW ON NOTUS

Democrats likely need strong third party candidates to win the Senate, NOTUS’ Paul Kane writes. In 2006, the party won three red state seats with pluralities after third party options pulled enough voters to matter. That flipped Senate control. This cycle, the Libertarian Party has candidates on the ballot in Iowa, Ohio and Texas, which will prove tempting for outside Democratic groups to try to support with independent expenditures, Paul writes.

But one of the Democratic beneficiaries of third party votes in 2006, former Sen. Claire McCaskill of Missouri, warns that the strategy could backfire. “If it is being manipulated and there are fingerprints, it can hurt,” she told Paul.

Of the 48,000 votes that went to the Libertarian in her 2006 race — helping secure her victory — McCaskill said, “That happened organically. We had nothing to do with it.”

More: Mike Rogers’ Pitch to Jewish Democrats May Be Falling Flat, by Jenna Monnin





NOT US

  • Maryland Gov. Wes Moore has spent 1 in 5 days of his term in other states, by Lee O. Sanderlin and Pamela Wood for The Baltimore Banner
  • ‘Have the balls to try’: The Democrats bucking AI skepticism, by Tyler Katzenberger for Politico
  • Election officials prepare for nightmare scenarios: Ballot seizures and violence, by Laura Barrón-López and Vaughn Hillyard for MS NOW
  • Trump wants a ballroom in Ireland. One man is having a ball fighting it. By Terrence McCoy for The Washington Post




Thank you for reading! If you liked this edition of the NOTUS Newsletter, please forward it to a friend. If this newsletter was shared with you, please sign up — it’s free! Have a tip? Email us at tips@notus.com. And as always, we’d love to hear your thoughts at newsletters@notus.com.

entries.title: From Watchdogs to ‘Lapdogs’: Inside the Trumpification of Agencies’ Inspectors General
entries.summary: Between canceled reports, deleted pages and mass firings, the government is getting less oversight.
entries.content:
The Veterans Affairs Department’s internal watchdog was set to relocate to a different Washington office space last year. That was until the inspector general decided she needed her own bathroom.

Cheryl Mason, who served as VA Secretary Doug Collins’ senior adviser before President Donald Trump fired the existing IG and tapped her to replace him, held up the move for months, citing the need for a personal lavatory in her office, three people familiar with the matter told NOTUS.

“She says that’s when people are at their most vulnerable moment,” and the lack of an en suite bathroom presented security concerns, an IG employee said. “They’re having to redesign the whole space.”

It’s the kind of potentially pricey request that government watchdogs typically investigate — and have in the past, like with former Housing Secretary Ben Carson’s office renovations in Trump’s first term.

The once-independent system that Congress established after Watergate has radically transformed in Trump’s second term. Trump’s unprecedented firing of nearly 20 inspectors general has unraveled the firewalls government’s ombudsmen have operated under for decades. The new watchdogs are erasing the lines between agency leadership and their own watchdog offices, Office of Inspector General employees told NOTUS, openly suggesting they should work hand-in-glove with the Trump administration to advance its goals.

“All the adults have left the room,” one senior OIG official said. “All these new IGs are lining up behind political leadership as if they're lapdogs.”

Trump has installed former political appointees from the same agencies they’re now overseeing, a co-author of Project 2025, and a Republican congressman into watchdog roles across the government. Those IGs have boosted the president and his appointees in ways that directly contravene the statutory independence of their offices, 11 current and former staffers told NOTUS.

Some offices are operating without a Senate-confirmed head, including the State Department, Environmental Protection Agency and USAID, all agencies where Trump fired former watchdogs early in his second term. There’s less oversight happening. Cabinet department OIGs issued 15% fewer audits and a quarter fewer investigative reports on average in the first half of this fiscal year compared to the same time period in every year from 2020 to 2024, according to the nonpartisan nonprofit Partnership for Public Service. These offices are down in staffing by nearly 20% on average.

As staff head for the exits across watchdog offices, those left are often operating within a culture of fear.

They’re “scared to death to do anything, so for the most part they're just sitting on their hands trying to lay low,” the senior OIG official said of acting career officials.

At the VA, Mason has boasted about her personal relationship to the secretary at virtually every meeting, four people familiar with her approach said. She heeded Collins’ requests on the timing and focus of some reports and repeatedly overruled career staff on final publications.

Mason denied requesting a bathroom in her new office, saying that all Senate-confirmed presidential appointees were required by law to have one. Through a spokesperson, she declined to say what law she was referring to and suggested NOTUS ask the General Services Administration. GSA was unable to point to any such law. There is a law that caps presidential appointees’ office renovation budgets to $5,000 — almost certainly too little to build a new bathroom.

***

Mason has leveraged her close ties to department leadership to make demands of staff.

After VA Secretary Collins’ office told the IG that preliminary alerts issued publicly by the watchdog on particularly alarming concerns were distracting senior staff, Mason eliminated them altogether, according to two people familiar with the edict. In an interview with NOTUS, Mason confirmed the change, saying the alerts were burdensome and not impactful.

She delayed reports on the modernization of electronic health records — a decades-long issue at VA — and limited discussion of staffing shortages in the office’s releases, again citing demands from the department. Mason told NOTUS her office was waiting for a clearer outline on the department’s workforce goals before raising any concerns about staffing cuts. VA medical staff who raised concerns about staffing shortages were merely presenting their “perception,” Mason said, and including those thoughts amounted to “hearsay.”

In at least one case, Mason struck entire sections from reports before they went public, according to draft copies provided to NOTUS. Those sections were about how the VA’s loss of primary care physicians impacted the overall system and were not included in the final report. Employees said the issue was flagged to them by staff during their investigation and should have been included, though Mason told them it was not within the scope of the report.

Mason has prevented staff from conducting the long-standing tradition of briefing Capitol Hill on its forthcoming reports, according to two people familiar with the change, telling employees the change was at Collins’ request. Prior to Mason taking the role, the IG would give a week’s notice to Congress’ veterans committees and proactively offer a briefing on any report that wasn’t routine, a Senate aide said. Now, Mason confirmed to NOTUS, she only provides a brief to the committees as they are releasing a report and only if committee members ask for one.

“It’s been incredibly challenging to continue doing the work we’re doing,” an employee said, who added that Mason asked if staff could bring items of concern to department leadership without publicly writing about them in reports.

Senior staff within the IG’s office were stunned by Mason’s requests, employees said.

“She wanted to make sure the message of everything we did was part of every agreement, promise or whatever she had with the secretary,” one employee said. “If you believe in independent oversight, that’s not what we were doing.”

Mason said her office has maintained its independence, though she noted she works “for the president of the United States,” is a part of VA and will continue to “work with the department.”

She acknowledged that she has changed her office’s approach, including to address issues raised by VA’s leadership. When Collins brings concerns to her, she said, she passes them along to staff but she alone has final decision-making authority.

“It’s not about ‘gotcha’ with the department,” Mason said.

She commissioned a flag for herself, telling staff she was serving in the equivalent role of a four-star general and therefore required one. One OIG employee said the flag cost more than $1,000.

“There,” Mason said, as she showed it to NOTUS over a video call. “Take a look at that flag.”

***

The 1978 Inspector General Act formally established the watchdog offices, and while it housed them within federal agencies and departments, required that they be “independent and objective.” Under the law, no agency official can prevent the IG from initiating an investigation, conducting its work or issuing a subpoena.

Employees across government said their offices are no longer operating within the parameters of that law.

Labor Department Inspector General Anthony D’Esposito, a former Republican congressman from New York, fired the career staffer who headed investigations in his office almost immediately after taking office, according to two people familiar with the move, which has not been previously reported.

That person had been spearheading a probe into an alleged inappropriate relationship between then-Labor Secretary Lori Chavez-DeRemer — a former Republican congresswoman who entered and exited the House with D’Esposito — and a staffer. Chavez-DeRemer has since stepped down from her post, and the report into her alleged misconduct has yet to come out.

D’Esposito’s office did not respond to a request for comment.

His messaging since his appointment has been unusually intertwined with that of the Trump administration. He has repeatedly praised Trump, reposts the official accounts of the White House, and wished Vice President JD Vance a “#HappyBirthday,” highlighting his leadership of the White House’s anti-fraud effort.

D’Esposito appeared alongside Trump at a campaign event in Nassau County, New York, last week.

“I have a clear message to everyone in New York state, Democrat, Republican, independent: You have no choice anymore but to vote Republican, vote Bruce Blakeman, vote every Republican you can find because the Democrats are destroying our state,” D’Esposito told the police academy audience. Blakeman is the Republican candidate running for governor of New York.
D'Esposito AP-26226652529538 (8155x5437, AR: 1.50)Larry Turner, D’Esposito’s predecessor who was fired by Trump, said his successor is “acting as an extension of a Cabinet member.” Turner served in four different IG offices and said he had never seen similar behavior.

“It’s a little dangerous because when you do that, what message does it say to your staff?” Turner said. “It makes them reluctant to write certain things.”

His former colleagues in the Labor Department’s IG office are trying to keep their heads down and do their jobs, he said, adding it’s now “a completely different environment.”

At the Education Department’s OIG, “nobody wants to speak up about anything,” a current employee told NOTUS. That’s despite what they said were staff concerns about the increasingly blurry relationship between the OIG and the agency.

The office’s deputy assistant inspector general for investigation services, Terry Harris, was moved from that investigative role to lead technology services — a change that stripped her of her law enforcement status, the Education OIG employee said.

“It’s got all the agents worried about doing anything that puts us on anyone’s radar,” they said.

The Education OIG declined to comment on the employee’s concerns.

The pressure to lay low is prevalent across the OIGs. A VA inspector general employee said anybody who gives feedback to Mason is labeled “a resister, and they are totally blackballed.”

“The president is restoring integrity and transparency to our federal government, which has long been neglected by previous administrations,” White House spokesperson Taylor Rogers told NOTUS in a statement, calling Trump’s nominees “highly-qualified and accomplished individuals.”
***

In a recent joint town hall with Housing and Urban Development staff and workers from its inspector general’s office, acting IG Brian Harrison, a career government employee whom Trump tapped to lead the agency on a temporary basis last August, said Congress envisioned agency watchdogs to serve as “the strong right arm of the secretary, not a distant entity far, far away.”

“The independence of the inspector general is intended to lessen friction, not increase friction,” Harrison said, according to a recording obtained by NOTUS. “Somehow, over the years, and I know it to be true that it's occurred here at HUD, that friction became friction between the IG and friction between the secretary. We don't do that at HUD OIG.”

Typically, watchdogs have gone to great lengths to avoid even the appearance of being political, officials said. Mike Missal, VA’s inspector general until Trump fired him last year, said comments like Harrison’s were antithetical to how he approached his role: “You never make friends in this job.”

“We're not supposed to use the office to support one side or the other. We are the umpires calling balls and strikes,” Mark Greenblatt, a former inspector general at the Interior Department who was fired by Trump, said. “You've co-opted the umpire and made them part of your team.”

Some Trump-appointed watchdogs have openly touted their collaboration with the administration as part of Trump’s “war on fraud.” Finding fraud is a core part of the inspector general mission, but the senior OIG official suggested some watchdogs are shattering norms and engaging in “political theater.”

“The new IGs, especially, are just going to meetings, standing at podiums, and saying, ‘We got more people that the Biden administration didn’t care about,’” they said, adding the watchdogs share talking points with White House officials. "You're clearly not independent if you're just repeating the vice president's quote.”

Even as the administration has boosted its involvement in the work of inspectors general, many IG offices have raised concerns about a lack of cooperation with their home departments.

Education’s previous acting IG René Rocque met with Education Secretary Linda McMahon last May to talk about “unreasonable denials and delays” as her office worked to review the massive staffing changes at the department last year. She was replaced shortly after that.

The final Education OIG report includes an entire section on the “scope limitation.” Another report issued this week included a similar caveat, saying the department wouldn’t give the OIG an org chart.

The Department of Homeland Security also delayed and denied requests for information from its watchdog over 20 times across six months last year, at times citing “management preference” for preventing the OIG from having access to the department, its watchdog said.

“Our results have not come easily,” a report from the DHS OIG last year says.

Those challenges are also being felt at the Government Accountability Office, which acts as Congress’ oversight research arm. Staff there are strategizing on how to obtain information from former agency employees or through informal channels, an employee said.

“We definitely did not start a couple jobs last year because they were not going to go anywhere,” the GAO employee said. NOTUS previously reported that some agencies will not comply with GAO inquiries if the probe originated with Democratic members of Congress.

“There are some conversations about how certain reports will be viewed by the administration,” the employee added. “There is just extra time on the tone, because of nervousness about it.”

Some oversight officials blamed lawmakers for failing to prevent Trump’s assault on oversight. So far, some Republicans in Congress have pushed to go in the opposite direction: A bill to abolish the centralized OIG Council of the Inspectors General on Integrity and Efficiency and move some of its responsibilities to the Office of Management and Budget has been making its way through the House with Republican support.

Current and former staff said they had never before heard the type of language they are now hearing from IGs, and it’s delivering a clear message to oversight staff.

“These firings — coupled with the self-censorship being practiced by many IG

offices — has reduced scrutiny of important issues like sole-source contracting and management abuses across the agencies,” said Paul Martin, a former inspector general at

USAID and NASA who was fired a day after his office released a report including warnings about the effects of dismantling USAID.

In some cases, employees are no longer publicizing issues that come up during their investigations.

“There is fear that writing something that is contrary to what the IG wants to put out there will lead to negative consequences,” another current senior official in an inspector general’s office said, adding that the administration has made clear what it wants from the watchdog offices. “Preventing that is exactly why the IGs were created.”
entries.author: Natalie Alms, Eric Katz

entries.title: Democrats Need Third-Party Help to Win Senate Majority
entries.summary: Democrats’ path to victory could require independent candidates peeling away conservative votes in several states.
entries.content:
Call them the 49 percent majority makers, a path blazed 20 years ago that Democrats probably need to replicate this fall.

Back in 2006, when they gained six seats and the Senate majority, Democrats relied on a trio of victories that came courtesy of a plurality: Claire McCaskill winning Missouri with 49.6 percent of the vote; Jon Tester winning Montana with 49.2 percent; and Jim Webb winning Virginia with 49.6 percent.

In each race, a small but significant bloc of voters ignored the two major parties’ candidates and cast ballots for independent options or wrote in their own alternative. Democratic challengers didn’t need to clear 50 percent to win in those solidly red states, opening the door for plurality victories and the narrowest possible majority, 51-49, in January 2007.

Two decades later, again needing wins in deeply conservative states, Democrats might have to get lucky in a few places with Republican-leaning voters who instead land on an independent candidate.

“In really close races, it can be the difference,” McCaskill, who served two Senate terms before losing in 2018, told NOTUS in an interview Thursday.

David Winston, a pollster who advised Senate Republican leaders in 2006, told NOTUS it’s difficult to really know who those voters would have preferred, as those are often just protest votes against both parties.

The real difference maker this fall will be whether voters who identify politically as independent remain as angry at Republicans as they were 20 years ago, according to Winston’s review of exit polling data. In 2006, those voters favored Democrats by 8 to 24 percentage points in Missouri, Montana and Virginia, the sort of margins that could spell doomsday for Republicans if they are replicated this fall.

“If Democrats win by double digits among independents and can sustain leads on the economy, a blue wave could be possible,” the Republican pollster said.

With Republicans holding 53 seats, Democrats need to flip four seats while defending all of their own to claim another 51-49 majority. North Carolina offers their ripest opportunity, as former Democratic Gov. Roy Cooper leads in public polling and has already won six statewide elections. Maine, which has voted Democratic in nine straight presidential elections, is their next objective with Sen. Susan Collins (R-Maine) locked in her usually tough fight.

Their next handful of targets — Alaska, Iowa, Nebraska, Ohio, Texas — all voted for President Donald Trump by double-digit margins two years ago. Even with his approval ratings sinking, Democratic candidates in these states will struggle to crest the 50-percent level if it’s truly a one-on-one race.

Using forecaster Nate Silver’s analysis, Democrat James Talarico leads Republican Ken Paxton in Texas in the average of polls, but the Democrat is barely above 47 percent. In Iowa, Democrat Josh Turek is statistically tied with Republican Rep. Ashley Hinson at almost 47 percent.

And in Ohio, Sherrod Brown has a narrow lead over the appointed Republican Sen. Jon Husted, but the former Democratic senator is still sitting just a hair over 49 percent in the polling averages.

Those Democrats appear to have locked down their party’s voters and independents willing to support them, but getting those last few percentage points to guarantee victory can be exceedingly difficult, especially in very large states.

Brown lost by just 3.5 percentage points in 2024, but he fell 207,000 votes shy of Sen. Bernie Moreno (R-Ohio). In 2018, Beto O’Rourke received enormous attention for his very close race against Sen. Ted Cruz (R-Texas), losing by about 2.5 percent. But the Democrat still came up 215,000 votes shy of Cruz.

Democratic chances will increase if a critical sliver of the usual Republican coalition either doesn’t show up or casts a protest vote for a third-party candidate. There’s some evidence that those types of Republican voters are out there: Republicans who do not identify with the MAGA label make up roughly 30 percent of the party’s coalition. Just 51 percent of those non-MAGA Republicans approve of the president’s job performance, according to this week’s Economist/YouGov poll.

And one key difference between now and 2006 is the dramatically looser campaign finance laws that allow super PACs to effectively serve as political boosters for the third-party candidates who might peel away votes.

Republicans in Alaska have accused Democrats of secretly supporting Dan J. Sullivan, a neophyte candidate who advanced to the November election this week, as a way to sabotage two-term Sen. Dan Sullivan’s reelection bid.

The Libertarian Party has candidates on the ballot in Iowa, Ohio and Texas, which will prove tempting for outside Democratic groups to try to support.

Ted Brown, a Libertarian activist for more than 45 years, might feel like a safe protest vote for a traditional Republican who is uncomfortable with scandal-plagued Paxton in November. As of the most recent federal filing, Brown’s campaign had raised less than $7,500 — with $5,000 of that coming from his own checkbook.

That’s probably an insufficient haul to run a high school student council race, let alone statewide in Texas, but some Democratic allies of Talarico will be tempted to try to fund an effort to persuade conservatives to back Brown.

McCaskill, however, warned that subterfuge could backfire if the lines back to one of the major party candidates were crystal clear, allowing an opponent to accuse the other campaign of trying to cheat.

“If it is being manipulated and there are fingerprints, it can hurt,” she said.

The most famous spoiler candidacies have happened at the presidential level, with many Democrats convinced that Ralph Nader’s Green Party candidacy crippled Al Gore’s White House bid in 2000. And Republicans remain bitter over billionaire Ross Perot’s 1992 campaign, denting support for George H.W. Bush’s re-election bid.

Just a few weeks ago, Mallory McMorrow’s name remained on the ballot in Michigan’s bitterly Democratic primary for the Senate. Abdul El-Sayed narrowly defeated Rep. Haley Stevens by less than 16,000 votes — while the zombie campaign of McMorrow received more than 61,000.

In 2006, even Republicans had grown tired of George W. Bush’s presidency, with the Iraq war in a slog and corruption cases that involved GOP lawmakers and administration officials. So some voters who would have normally pulled the Republican lever found other alternatives.

“That happened organically. We had nothing to do with it,” McCaskill recalled of the nearly 48,000 votes that went to the Libertarian that year in Missouri.

Her margin of victory was about 49,000, out of more than 2.1 million cast, and a more liberal third-party candidate pulled 17,000 votes.

Webb, who had served as Navy secretary during the Reagan administration, defeated the incumbent, George Allen, by a little more than 9,000 votes while a liberal leaning independent candidate received more than 26,000 votes and almost 2,500 wrote in another candidate.

Tester had the clearest benefit from a Libertarian on the ballot. Tester won by about 3,500 votes over a scandal-plagued incumbent, and the more conservative Libertarian pulled more than 10,000 votes.

Six years later, Tester won with barely 48 percent of the vote after allies ran a pretty direct campaign to boost the Libertarian candidate.

Winston, the pollster, said Republicans would not have any worries if they simply could answer the economic concerns of voters not registered with either major party. That would seal victory without fearing third-party confusion as a factor.

“The key question is, again,” he told NOTUS, “where are independents?”
entries.author: Paul Kane

entries.title: Log Cabin Republicans Officially Drop the “T” from LGBT
entries.summary: The group, which represents gay conservatives, echoed the president’s hard-line stance against what it called “radical gender ideology.”
entries.content:
Log Cabin Republicans, the nation’s largest group representing gay conservatives and their allies, will no longer advocate for transgender rights, a senior leader for the organization announced in a column Thursday.

Ross Hemminger, the group’s president, wrote that the organization’s board of directors voted to narrow its national advocacy focus on issues relating to sexual orientation and conservative values. The group will now focus on lesbian, gay and bisexual advocacy, officially dropping the “T” from the widely used acronym LGBT.

“We are an LGB advocacy organization,” Hemminger said, “as our founders envisioned and as our moral center calls us to be.”

The federal government has significantly rolled back transgender rights since President Donald Trump’s return to office. Trump has pushed to remove federal funding for gender-affirming care for minors, pressured schools to remove transgender student athletes from women’s sports and issued an executive order that all passports must reflect an individual’s assigned sex at birth.

Hemminger embraced Trump and hard-right conservatives’ anti-trans arguments in his column, writing that the “transgender movement” seeks to push schools to teach “radical gender ideology” and supports gender affirming care for minors.

GLAAD, an LGBT+ media advocacy organization, has pushed back against that framing and said that use of the phrase “trans agenda” by right-wing media figures and politicians frames “the pursuit of visibility and basic rights — such as access to healthcare and public safety — as sinister or threatening.”

Log Cabin Republicans voted to include transgender Americans as a part of their advocacy in 2015 “out of a belief that all adults should be allowed to pursue their own happiness” as long as it did not “impede on the inalienable rights of others,” Hemminger said.

“At the time, we did not believe that we would find ourselves where we are today,” Hemminger continued.

Hemminger said that the shift away from transgender advocacy does not change who can join the Log Cabin Republicans. The group has maintained a close relationship with First Lady Melania Trump, who made rare public appearances during the 2024 election cycle to host a fundraiser for the group and speak at one of its events.

The first lady’s office did not immediately return to a request for comment on the Log Cabin Republicans’ new national focus.
entries.author: Angie Orellana Hernandez
